speaker_role: current admissions officer (Lee Coffin, Dartmouth's dean of admissions) interviewed by independent counselors/podcast hosts, one of whom runs a paid counseling firm
commercial_incentive: hosts run a paid college-counseling firm (School Match 4U) and the podcast promotes paid coaching sessions; the Coffin interview segment itself is not a sales pitch
key_insights: Lee Coffin frames Dartmouth's identity via 'place, program, people': a rural setting driving environmental/sustainability academic strength, small classes (about two-thirds under 12 students), and a quarter system enabling flexible, self-directed academic paths
Coffin states personal qualities (curiosity, kindness, creativity, collaboration) meaningfully drive admit decisions even though they cannot be quantified or reported like GPA/SAT
Evidence of personal qualities is gathered mainly through essays, recommendations, and interviews/introductions, not the extracurricular list itself
Dartmouth's aid is described as need-blind, meeting full need, with no loans, full coverage of off-campus study, and no parent contribution for the lowest-income families

Hosts separately discuss that colleges track yield data by region, major, and GPA band, and some schools have identified specific applicant profiles with under-1% predicted yield, influencing admit decisions ('yield protection')
Hosts describe real named schools (University of Denver, St. Olaf, High Point) now offering explicit scholarships or benefits specifically for Early Decision applicants to lock in yield
specific_numbers_or_facts: St. Olaf guarantees a minimum $20,000 scholarship to any student admitted via Early Decision (quoted from St. Olaf's website by host)
High Point offers free tuition to 10 different master's programs for undergraduates who apply ED, starting with the class of 2024 (per host)
About two-thirds of Dartmouth's courses have 12 students or fewer (Lee Coffin)
notable_or_distinctive: a sitting Ivy League admissions dean states on record that unmeasurable personal-quality evidence meaningfully drives admit decisions, paired with candid host discussion of specific named schools now paying students to apply Early Decision
reliability_notes: long podcast (9,682 words) with substantial unrelated tangents (program cuts, humanities enrollment, a GPA-dip scenario) before the Dartmouth interview; Coffin's content is credible first-person testimony, but host commentary on other schools' ED incentives is their own secondhand interpretation
